lesson.title: Straight Up: Vertical Tangent Points
lesson.summary: A vertical tangent point occurs where a continuous curve has a genuine tangent line, but that line is vertical because the one-sided derivatives both diverge to the same infinite sign.
lesson.body:
A vertical tangent point is the gentlest member of the non-differentiable family, precisely because the curve still has something that deserves to be called a tangent line at that point, it is just a vertical one, and a vertical line has no finite slope to serve as a derivative. This happens when both one-sided derivatives diverge to infinity with the same sign, rather than opposite signs as in a cusp. Because the sign agrees on both sides, the curve does not turn back on itself; it passes smoothly through the point, momentarily standing straight up as it does, the way an S-shaped curve can flatten into verticality for just an instant before continuing on its way.

The standard example is the cube root function, f(x) = x^(1/3), evaluated at a = 0. Using the power rule, f'(x) = (1/3) times x raised to the power -2/3, which can be written as 1 divided by 3 times x^(2/3). Since x^(2/3) is the cube root of x squared, and squaring erases any negative sign, x^(2/3) is positive for every nonzero x, whether x itself is positive or negative. That means f'(x) is positive on both sides of 0. As x approaches 0 from either direction, x^(2/3) shrinks toward 0, so f'(x) = 1 / (3 x^(2/3)) grows without bound toward positive infinity from both the left and the right.

Because both one-sided derivatives diverge to the same sign, positive infinity on each side, this is a vertical tangent point rather than a cusp. The graph of x^(1/3) is a continuous, strictly increasing S-shaped curve that passes through the origin standing perfectly vertical at that one instant, then continues climbing smoothly on both sides. There is no kink and no doubling back, just a single point where the slope, instead of being some finite number, is effectively infinite.

This distinction between vertical tangent points and cusps is exactly the same test used earlier, checking whether the two infinite one-sided derivatives share a sign or not, and it connects directly to the definition of a tangent line at ordinary points. An ordinary tangent line is defined as the limiting position of secant lines through nearby points on the curve; at a vertical tangent point, that same limiting process still produces a well-defined limiting line, it simply happens to be vertical, with equation x = a rather than y = (something)(x - a) + f(a). The derivative fails to exist only because a vertical line cannot be written in slope-intercept form, not because the geometric notion of a tangent line breaks down.

Recognizing a vertical tangent point from a formula follows the same routine as the other non-differentiable cases: differentiate, evaluate the one-sided limits as x approaches the suspicious point, and check whether they blow up to infinity. If they do, and if the sign matches on both sides, the graph has a vertical tangent there rather than a cusp or a corner, and it is worth remembering that despite the missing derivative, the curve itself remains smooth and continuous through that single vertical instant.
